Top candidates: White_Mold (white cottony growth), Diaporthe (black specks on stems), Green_stem_disorder.

Let me check reference images for the top candidates.

White Mold reference matches very well — the top-left panel shows fluffy grayish-white mycelial growth at the node, identical to the test image. Let me check more references to meet the minimum requirement.

All other candidates are ruled out. The analysis is clear:

**Test image:** Shows a soybean stem node with grayish-white fluffy/cottony mycelial growth at the junction. Stem remains green externally. Background leaves are yellowing.

**White Mold match:** The White Mold reference image (top-left panel) shows nearly identical fluffy gray-white fungal mycelium growing at the stem node — an exact visual match. White mold (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) characteristically produces this cottony white mycelium at nodes on otherwise green-looking stems, with surrounding leaf senescence.

**Why other candidates are ruled out:**
- Diaporthe: Brown dead stems with linear black specks — no fluffy growth
- Brown Stem Rot: Internal pith browning, not external mycelial growth
- Sudden Death Syndrome: Interveinal chlorosis on leaves, white pith internally
- Charcoal Rot: Grayish discoloration from microsclerotia, not cottony mycelium
- Powdery Mildew: White powder on leaf surfaces, not stem nodes
